- Writing test scenarios (happy path, edge cases, error handling)
- Setting up test fixtures
- Running the tests in CI

For each module, I'd estimate maybe 4-8 hours of work depending on complexity.

technical_and_design_decisions: Use JUnit 5 (Jupiter) as the test framework, consistent with modern Spring projects (Spring Framework 6.x / Spring Boot 3.x baseline).
Reuse the existing Spring Cloud Stream App Starters / Spring Cloud Data Flow acceptance-test pattern (deploy app, send/receive messages, assert side-effects).
Use AssertJ for fluent assertions, in line with the Spring ecosystem defaults.
Use a stub/mock HTTP server (e.g., MockWebServer / WireMock) for the Splunk sink instead of a real Splunk instance, so the CI build is self-contained.
Use Testcontainers only if absolutely necessary; otherwise prefer in-process mocks to keep CI runtime low.
Use Apache Spark's local-mode / shared testing utilities for the spark-app batch job to avoid requiring a Spark cluster in CI.
Integrate tests via Maven Failsafe (so they run during the 'verify' phase) wired into the existing CI build pipeline.
Group module-level tests under a common acceptance-tests source set so they share a common harness (Spring context, message broker, base class).
Keep each module's tests independent (one JUnit class per user story) to allow granular failure reporting in CI.
Treat 'null' sink as a true no-op verification; treat 'splunk' and 'spark-app' as the highest-complexity targets.
assumptions: The eight sink/batch modules already have working production code; this increment adds only acceptance-test coverage, not new features.
A common acceptance-test harness, message broker fixture (e.g., embedded broker), and base Spring configuration already exist or can be lightly extended; otherwise they are created as part of A1.
The CI build infrastructure (Jenkins/GitHub Actions pipeline, JDK 17, Maven) is already in place; the work only configures the new test module into the existing pipeline.
Each module is exercised with 3-6 representative acceptance scenarios (happy path + 2-5 edge cases), typical for this style of coverage.
External services (Splunk HEC, shell environment, file system) are mocked or stubbed so the build remains hermetic and fast (<10 min total added CI time).
Effort figures represent an experienced Java/Spring developer familiar with Spring Cloud Stream/Data Flow concepts and the existing codebase.
Effort includes writing, locally verifying, and stabilizing the tests, but excludes triaging pre-existing product bugs surfaced by the new tests (those would be filed separately).

activities.activity_description: Create/extend a shared acceptance-tests Maven module: add Failsafe plugin configuration, base Spring test context, message broker fixture, common utility classes, JUnit 5/AssertJ dependencies, and wire the new tests into the existing CI pipeline (run on every build, publish JUnit reports).
Implement acceptance tests verifying that the null sink consumes messages without error, produces no output, preserves message count semantics, and handles null payloads and empty streams correctly.

Implement acceptance tests verifying that the rich_gauge sink publishes the expected gauge metric values (name, value, tags, timestamp) under various input scenarios, using an in-process metrics registry to capture and assert emissions.

Implement acceptance tests verifying the router sink's expression-based routing: messages are dispatched to the correct named destinations and dropped when no route matches, covering both SpEL and property-placeholder expression variants.

Implement acceptance tests verifying that the shell sink correctly invokes the configured command/script, passes the message payload (stdin), captures stdout, and handles non-zero exit codes and timeouts gracefully. Uses temporary scripts and a controlled working directory.

Implement acceptance tests verifying that the splunk sink formats and POSTs events to the Splunk HEC endpoint with the expected URL, headers, token, and JSON body. Uses an embedded HTTP mock server (WireMock/MockWebServer) to capture and assert the outbound requests, including batching and error responses.

Implement acceptance tests verifying the throughput-sampler sink's sampling rate: with a deterministic source, the ratio of forwarded vs. dropped messages approximates the configured rate within an acceptable tolerance, and edge cases (rate=0, rate=1) are handled.

activities.activity_name: Acceptance tests for spark-app batch job (U7)
activities.activity_description: Implement acceptance tests verifying the spark-app batch job end-to-end: job launch, Spark context bootstrap, input ingestion, transformation, and output emission. Uses Spark local mode and a small synthetic dataset to keep CI runtime reasonable; covers success and failure exit codes.

activities.activity_name: Acceptance tests for timestampfile batch job (U8)
activities.activity_description: Implement acceptance tests verifying that the timestampfile batch job reads the configured source(s), applies the timestamp-based logic, and writes the expected output file(s) with correct naming, content, and timestamp semantics. Uses a temp directory for isolation.

Run the full acceptance suite end-to-end in the CI environment, triage and fix any flaky tests, ensure stable execution order and resource cleanup, update the module README/CI docs to describe how to run the new tests, and confirm a green build from a clean checkout.
